subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Compression and Power
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Compression and Power.

hook.text: The more you squeeze the fuel-air mix before igniting it, the more energy you extract.

buildup.text: Compression ratio measures how tightly the piston squeezes the mix inside the cylinder.

discovery.text: A ratio of 10:1 means the mix shrinks to one-tenth its volume before the spark fires.

twist.text: Push too high and the fuel ignites on its own before the spark—a destructive event called knock.

climax.text: Engineers balance compression ratio against knock to extract peak power without damage.

punchline.text: Squeezing harder makes power until the engine fights back.

details.summary: An engine's compression ratio determines how much it squeezes the air-fuel mixture before ignition, with higher ratios extracting more energy from each combustion event but requiring higher-octane fuel to prevent knocking.
details.whyItMatters: Compression ratio is a fundamental lever for engine efficiency. Understanding it explains why diesel engines are more efficient than gasoline engines and why premium fuel exists for performance cars.
takeaways: Higher compression extracts more work from each combustion cycle
Typical gasoline engines have 10:1 to 13:1 compression ratios
Diesel engines achieve 15:1 to 22:1 ratios for higher efficiency

faq.question: Why does higher compression require premium fuel?
faq.answer: High compression heats the air-fuel mixture more, risking premature detonation called knocking. Higher-octane fuel resists detonation at these elevated temperatures, protecting the engine from damaging pressure spikes.

faq.question: Is there a limit to how high compression ratios can go?
faq.answer: Yes. At extreme ratios, the fuel detonates uncontrollably regardless of octane. Material strength and thermal limits also constrain maximum compression. Mazda's Skyactiv-X pushes gasoline compression to 16:1 using innovative control.
